newsitem.title: INDIA: India considers raising diesel, kerosene prices.
newsitem.headline: India considers raising diesel, kerosene prices.

text.p: The Indian government has tentatively decided to raise the prices of diesel and kerosene with a plan that would trim about $1.5 billion from a subsidy bill but spare petrol users, newspapers said on Tuesday.

They said the government, keen to plug the gap between world and domestic prices which leads to rising subsidies, has also tentatively agreed to phase out the administered price mechanism which keeps Indian prices below international levels.
They said Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, who is also petroleum minister, had endorsed the plan which they said would be presented to the 15-party United Front coalition on Sunday.

Gujral's centre-left alliance would have to approve the package before it could be implemented. Left-wing parties in the coalition have come out against price increases and are especially opposed to a rise in the cost of kerosene.
But because of the burgeoning cost of subsidising the prices of petroleum products, the government owes oil companies more than 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion), according to official estimates.
The Economic Times said that under the plan, kerosene prices would be increased by 20 percent, while those of high speed diesel and liquified petroleum gas (LPG) would be raised by 15 percent.
The price increases would reduce the government's outstanding oil subsidy bill, called the oil pool deficit, by about 55 billion rupees, it said.
The Times of India said there would be no increase in the prices of either petrol or aviation turbine fuel.
The subsidies on high speed diesel and LPG would be phased out over two and three years, respectively, it said.
Subsidies for kerosene, which currently are applied to the oil pool account, would be shifted to the general budget within five years, the Economic Times said.

The newspaper said currently the domestic prices of diesel and kerosene are well below their international levels. Domestic petrol costs more, and money earned from the difference between the price in India and on the international market partially offsets the cost of subsidising diesel and kerosene.
The Times of India said the oil pool deficit was projected to rise to 245 billion rupees by March 31, 1998 if the prices of petroleum products were left unchanged.

It said the government had rejected a proposal to reduce the customs and excise duties on crude oil and other petroleum products as that would lead to a cut in government revenues and increase the fiscal deficit.
Government officials were unavailable for comment.
